name: Grand Portage agreement under the Nelson Act, signed October 24, 1889
aka: Nelson Act cession, Grand Portage band
Act for the relief and civilization of the Chippewa Indians in the State of Minnesota (Nelson Act)
citation: Act of January 14, 1889, ch. 24, 25 Stat. 642; agreement printed in H. R. Ex. Doc. 247, 51st Cong., 1st sess.
nations: Grand Portage Band of Lake Superior Chippewa
promises: Section 1: an Indian already holding an allotment on the reservation not to be deprived of it or disturbed except by his own separate consent; the cession valid only if assented to in writing by two-thirds of the band's male adults.
Section 3: allotments in severalty; any Indian could take his allotment on the reservation where he lived instead of removing to White Earth.
Sections 4 and 5: pine lands examined, appraised at no less than $3 per thousand feet of timber, and sold at public auction in 40-acre lots for no less than the appraised value.
Section 6: other ceded land sold only to actual settlers under the homestead law at $1.25 an acre.

Section 7: all net proceeds held in the Treasury as a permanent fund for all the Chippewa in Minnesota at 5% interest, paid yearly for fifty years, with a quarter of the interest for schools, and the fund then divided among them in equal shares.

breaches.what: The Minnesota Chippewa Tribe, of which the Grand Portage Band is a member, claimed in Indian Claims Commission Dockets 19 and 188 that Nelson Act land and timber proceeds were misspent and that land and timber were sold for less than full value. The claims were settled for $20 million, which the Court of Federal Claims awarded in May 1999.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Minnesota Chippewa Tribe v. United States, Dockets 19 and 188 (settlement), as described in the Bureau of Indian Affairs' testimony to the House Subcommittee on Indian and Alaska Native Affairs, March 1, 2012

breaches.what: The Grand Portage Band states that the Nelson Act of 1889, together with the Dawes Act, allowed speculators to grab large portions of its reservation land.

landTaken: Royce records that the band ceded to the United States all its title and interest in the Grand Portage reservation (Royce area 339, set apart by the 1854 treaty), and its interest in the part of the Red Lake reservation not needed for allotments. Under the Act, land not allotted was to be sold for the Chippewa fund.
compensation: The net proceeds of sales were to go into the Chippewa permanent fund (Section 7). The Bureau of Indian Affairs testified in 2012 that after the fifty years there were no remaining funds to distribute in equal shares. The 1999 settlement of $20 million covers all six member bands of the Minnesota Chippewa Tribe.
today: Royce, writing in 1899, describes area 339 as the present Grand Portage reserve. In 2012 the Bureau of Indian Affairs supported a bill to distribute the 1999 settlement funds, then held in trust, and noted that the Leech Lake Band opposed its formula. Whether the bill became law was not checked.

plain.promised: Allotments where people lived, no one's allotment taken without consent, and all land and timber sale money held in a fund for all Minnesota Chippewa at 5% interest for fifty years, then shared equally.
plain.happened: The Minnesota Chippewa Tribe, which includes the Grand Portage Band, claimed the sale money was misspent and land and timber sold below full value. No formal finding specific to this cession has been located.
plain.today: The claims were settled for $20 million in 1999, covering all six member bands. The Bureau of Indian Affairs said in 2012 no fund was left to share out. Whether the settlement money was distributed was not checked.

nationVoice.nation: Grand Portage Band of Lake Superior Chippewa
nationVoice.summary: The Band says the 1854 treaty set aside Grand Portage as one of two small reservations, that the Dawes Act of 1887 and the Nelson Act of 1889 let speculators take large parts of the reservation, and that the tribe has since bought some of that land back.

openQuestions: treaties.json error: presentDayTribes for this entry lists eight bands but not the Grand Portage Band of Lake Superior Chippewa, the band that signed it. The scheduleTribes name 'Chippewa of the Mississippi and Lake Superior' is generic; Royce's schedule names the Grand Portage Chippewa.
The 1999 settlement is a compromise and is recorded as litigation, not a finding. No court or Commission finding specific to the Grand Portage cession was found.
The agreement itself (H. R. Ex. Doc. 247, 51st Cong., 1st sess.) was not opened; the date and terms are from Royce and the Act.
Whether the Grand Portage band's land was in fact ceded entire, as Royce's wording says, or kept as allotments with only the surplus sold, was not established; the reservation exists today.

Audit 2026-11-08: removed the stale open question saying the Grand Portage Band's own account was not found; the file now cites the Band's Our Heritage page, which was opened and says the Dawes and Nelson Acts allowed speculators to grab up large portions of reservation land.
